- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.7) and forecast is rising steadily, cap upward momentum to avoid over-optimism; if sentiment turns negative, reduce forecast slope.
- If true outcome shows sharp spike followed by sharp drop (e.g., 80+ to 70+), model often over-anticipates and overshoots — apply downward correction after spike.
- In low-sentiment periods (e.g., sentiment <0.3), model tends to underreact — increase forecast baseline slightly to avoid underestimating downside risk.
- When history shows mean reversion (e.g., recent prices near 75–80, then true outcome drops below 75), model often fails to recognize it — adjust forecast to reflect mean-reversion bias.
- For 30-day horizon, if sentiment is volatile or mixed, model should not assume smooth trend — introduce smoothing or lagged adjustment to avoid overfitting to recent highs.
- If sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., < -0.4) and forecast is rising, reverse direction or reduce slope — negative sentiment often signals market correction.
- In cases where true outcome deviates sharply from forecast mid-horizon (e.g., 78.5 → 87.8), model may be ignoring sentiment shifts — check sentiment 3–5 days prior for signal of reversal or breakout.
